The focus shifts to crafting a CUDA C++ solver for 3D spherical ideal-MHD with a compositional passive scalar. Accuracy hinges on meticulously verifying the underlying physics, mathematical formulation, unit system, and numerical methods embedded within this solver.


A unit system is required to ensure that the variables remain O(1) in floating point, preventing overflow or underflow. Considering the RTX 4080 SUPER's capabilities, the memory footprint and performance of both single and double precision needs assessment. The MHD update's memory-bandwidth-bound nature suggests careful consideration of FP64 performance for optimal efficiency with the given cell count and FLOPs per step.


Using `double` precision should eliminate roundoff errors in critical calculations like spherical volumes, potentially preserving equilibrium. Double precision should ensure high-fidelity conservation of mass, momentum, and energy. A test will verify these claims, focusing on verifying the core MHD solver `heliomhd3d.cu` after compilation.

Code units are defined as: length $L_0 = 1\text{ AU}$, velocity $V_0 = 100\text{ km/s}$, and time $t_0 = L_0/V_0$. The radial boundaries are set to $0.1\ L_0$ and $2.4\ L_0$, covering the region of interest.


Calculating dimensionless parameters for the unit system, specifically the solar gravitational parameter and defining the proton number density. The dimensionless solar gravitational parameter, $\tilde{\mu}_\odot$, is derived from the dimensional gravitational constant and chosen units. The proton number density unit, $n_0$, is set to $1.0\text{ cm}^{-3}$ for use in the dimensionless equations.

The mass density unit, $\rho_0$, is determined from the proton number density unit and proton mass, accounting for 5% Helium, which results in a mean ion mass. The pressure unit, $P_0$, is then defined using the derived mass density unit and velocity unit. These units will ensure the physical variables are appropriately scaled.


The dimensionless pressure is derived, and a check confirms the sound speed scaling.  The magnetic field unit, B₀, is calculated using the defined units and checked against the Alfvén speed, finding agreement.  The resulting unit system provides straightforward scaling for radial distance, density, and velocity.


A dimensionless temperature scale is derived from the established units and is linked to the density for pressure computation. The magnetic field is also scaled based on the defined units.

Five operational modes will be incorporated into the MHD solver to facilitate comprehensive testing. The first mode implements the Brio & Wu shock tube benchmark for validation.


Additional operational modes are planned to enable comprehensive testing of the MHD solver. One mode will incorporate polytropic temperature scaling and passive heavy-ion scalar conservation. Another will enable comparison against a 1D radial steady MHD ODE solution. The tilted-CIR mode will replicate the literature benchmark. A full 3D time-dependent heliospheric MHD simulation mode will also be included.


The solver will model the November-December 2025 solar wind extending to 2.4 AU.  It will be configurable with various boundary conditions, grid resolutions, polytropic indices, and optional CME injection or solar gravity. The simulation will first relax to a quasi-steady state, followed by time-dependent evolution, and high-cadence data sampling. High-cadence data will be generated along the trajectories of several spacecraft including 3I/ATLAS, STEREO-A, Solar Orbiter, Wind, and ACE.
